verses.text: After Saul died, David returned from defeating the Amalekites and spent two days in Ziklag.
On the third day a man arrived from Saul's camp with torn clothes and dirt on his head. When he reached David, he fell to the ground and bowed.
David asked, “Where have you come from?” He answered, “I escaped from Israel's camp.”
David asked, “What happened? Tell me.” He said, “Our troops ran from the battle, and many fell and died. Saul and his son Jonathan are dead too.”
David asked the young man, “How do you know Saul and Jonathan are dead?”
He said, “I happened to be on Mount Gilboa and saw Saul leaning on his spear. The chariots and horsemen were closing in on him.
He looked back, saw me, and called to me. I answered, ‘Here I am.’
He asked, ‘Who are you?’ I told him, ‘I'm an Amalekite.’
He said, ‘Come over here and kill me, please. I'm in agony, and I'm still alive.’
So I went over and killed him because I was sure he wouldn't survive after what had happened. I took the crown from his head and the bracelet from his arm and brought them here to you, my lord.”
David grabbed his clothes and tore them, and all the men with him did the same.
They mourned, wept, and fasted until evening for Saul and Jonathan, for the LORD's people, and for the house of Israel, because they'd fallen by the sword.
David asked the young man who brought him the news, “Where are you from?” He said, “I'm the son of a foreigner, an Amalekite.”
David asked, “Why weren't you afraid to raise your hand against the LORD's anointed and kill him?”
David called one of his young men and told him to strike the messenger down. The man struck him, and he died.
David said, “Your blood is on your own head. Your own words testified against you when you said, ‘I killed the LORD's anointed.’”
David sang this lament for Saul and his son Jonathan.
He told the people to teach the children of Judah the Song of the Bow, which is written in the Book of Jashar.
“Israel, your glory lies slain on your heights. How the mighty have fallen!
Don't tell it in Gath or announce it in the streets of Ashkelon. The daughters of the Philistines will celebrate, and the daughters of the uncircumcised will shout for joy.
Mountains of Gilboa, may no dew or rain fall on you and no fields yield offerings. There the mighty man's shield was defiled and cast away. Saul's shield lies without its oil.
From the blood of the fallen and the fat of the mighty, Jonathan's bow never turned back. Saul's sword never came home empty.
Saul and Jonathan were loved and admired in life, and death didn't separate them. They were faster than eagles and stronger than lions.
Daughters of Israel, weep for Saul. He dressed you in fine scarlet and put gold ornaments on your clothes.
How the mighty have fallen in the middle of battle! Jonathan lies slain on your heights.
I'm grieving for you, Jonathan, my brother. You were so dear to me. Your love for me was wonderful, beyond the love of women.
How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war have perished!”
After this David asked the LORD, “Should I go up to one of Judah's towns?” The LORD said, “Go up.” David asked where, and the LORD said, “To Hebron.”
So David went up with his two wives, Ahinoam from Jezreel and Abigail, the widow of Nabal from Carmel.
He brought his men and their households too. They settled in the towns around Hebron.
The men of Judah came and anointed David king over Judah. They told him, “The men of Jabesh Gilead buried Saul.”
David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh Gilead and said, “May the LORD bless you for showing this kindness to Saul, your lord, by burying him.
May the LORD show you faithful love and loyalty. I'll also repay you for the kindness you've shown.
Now be strong and brave. Saul your lord is dead, and the people of Judah have anointed me king over them.”
Meanwhile Abner son of Ner, Saul's army commander, took Saul's son Ishbosheth to Mahanaim.
He made him king over Gilead, the Ashurites, Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin, and all Israel.
Saul's son Ishbosheth was forty when he became king over Israel. He reigned two years, while Judah followed David.
David reigned over Judah at Hebron for seven years and six months.
Abner son of Ner and the men of Saul's son Ishbosheth went from Mahanaim to Gibeon.
Joab son of Zeruiah and David's men met them at the pool of Gibeon. The two groups sat on opposite sides of the pool.
Abner told Joab, “Let's have the young men get up and compete in front of us.” Joab answered, “Let them get up.”
Twelve men stepped forward for Benjamin and Saul's son Ishbosheth, and twelve stepped forward for David.
Each grabbed his opponent by the head and drove his sword into the other's side. They all fell together, so that place at Gibeon was called Helkath Hazzurim.
The battle was fierce that day. David's men defeated Abner and the army of Israel.
Zeruiah's three sons were there: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Asahel could run as fast as a wild gazelle.
Asahel chased Abner, refusing to turn aside to the right or left.
Abner looked back and asked, “Is that you, Asahel?” He answered, “It is.”
Abner told him, “Turn aside and take the armor of one of the young men.” But Asahel refused to stop chasing him.
Abner told him again, “Stop following me. Why should I strike you down? How could I face your brother Joab afterward?”
Asahel still refused. Abner struck him with the back end of his spear, and Asahel died where he fell. Everyone who came to that spot stopped.
Joab and Abishai kept chasing Abner. The sun went down as they reached the hill of Ammah opposite Giah, on the road toward the wilderness of Gibeon.
The Benjaminites rallied behind Abner and stood together on a hilltop.
Abner called to Joab, “Will the sword keep devouring forever? Don't you see how bitter this will end? How long will you wait before telling your men to stop chasing their own brothers?”
Joab said, “As surely as God lives, if you hadn't spoken, my men would have kept chasing their brothers until morning.”
Joab blew the trumpet, and everyone stopped. They gave up the chase and stopped fighting Israel.
Abner and his men marched through the Arabah all night, crossed the Jordan, went through all of Bithron, and reached Mahanaim.
Joab came back from chasing Abner and gathered his men. Nineteen of David's men were missing, besides Asahel.
David's men had killed three hundred sixty of the Benjaminites and Abner's men.
They took Asahel and buried him in his father's tomb at Bethlehem. Joab and his men traveled through the night and reached Hebron at daybreak.
The war between Saul's house and David's house went on for a long time. David grew stronger and stronger, while Saul's family grew weaker and weaker.
David had sons in Hebron. His firstborn was Amnon, whose mother was Ahinoam from Jezreel.
His second was Chileab, whose mother was Abigail, the widow of Nabal from Carmel. His third was Absalom, whose mother was Maacah daughter of King Talmai of Geshur.
His fourth was Adonijah son of Haggith, and his fifth was Shephatiah son of Abital.
His sixth was Ithream, whose mother was David's wife Eglah. These sons were born to David in Hebron.
During the war between Saul's and David's households, Abner gained power in Saul's house.
Saul had a concubine named Rizpah daughter of Aiah. Ishbosheth asked Abner, “Why did you sleep with my father's concubine?”

Abner was furious at what Ishbosheth said. “Am I some dog serving Judah? I've been loyal to your father Saul's family, his brothers, and his friends. I haven't handed you over to David, and now you accuse me of wrongdoing over this woman?
May God deal with me, Abner, as severely as he sees fit if I fail to do for David what the LORD swore to do for him:
take the kingdom away from Saul's family and establish David's throne over Israel and Judah, from Dan to Beersheba.”
Ishbosheth was too afraid of Abner to say another word.
Abner sent messengers to David on his behalf. “Who does the land belong to? Make an alliance with me, and I'll help bring all Israel over to your side.”
David said, “Good. I'll make a treaty with you on one condition. Don't come to see me unless you bring Saul's daughter Michal with you.”
David sent messengers to Saul's son Ishbosheth demanding, “Give me back my wife Michal. I paid a hundred Philistine foreskins to marry her.”
Ishbosheth sent men to take her away from her husband, Paltiel son of Laish.
Paltiel followed her, weeping all the way to Bahurim. Abner told him, “Go back home.” So he went back.
Abner told Israel's elders, “You've wanted David as your king for some time.
Now make it happen. The LORD has said about David, ‘Through my servant David I'll rescue my people Israel from the Philistines and all their enemies.’”
Abner also spoke to Benjamin's people. Then he went to Hebron to tell David what Israel and the whole tribe of Benjamin had agreed to.
Abner came to David at Hebron with twenty men. David gave a feast for Abner and his men.
Abner told David, “I'll go and gather all Israel to you, my lord the king. They'll make a covenant with you, and you'll rule over all you desire.” David sent Abner on his way, and he left in peace.
Just then Joab and David's men came back from a raid with a great deal of plunder. Abner was no longer with David at Hebron, because David had sent him away in peace.
When Joab and all his troops arrived, they told him Abner son of Ner had come to the king and had been sent away in peace.
Joab went to the king and said, “What have you done? Abner came here to you. Why did you let him get away?
You know Abner son of Ner. He came to trick you, find out where you go and when you return, and learn everything you're doing.”
After leaving David, Joab sent messengers after Abner. They brought him back from the well of Sirah, but David knew nothing about it.
When Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside inside the gate as if to speak privately with him. There he killed Abner to avenge his brother Asahel.
When David heard about it, he said, “My kingdom and I are forever innocent before the LORD of the blood of Abner son of Ner.

May it fall on Joab and his entire family. May there always be someone in Joab's house with a discharge or a serious skin disease, someone who leans on a staff, falls by the sword, or goes without bread.”
Joab and his brother Abishai killed Abner because he had killed their brother Asahel in the battle at Gibeon.
David ordered Joab and everyone with him to tear their clothes, put on sackcloth, and mourn for Abner. King David himself walked behind the funeral bier.
They buried Abner in Hebron. The king cried out and wept at his grave, and all the people wept.
The king sang a lament for Abner. “Should Abner have died like a fool?
Your hands were free, and your feet weren't in chains. You fell as someone falls at the hands of wicked men.” All the people wept for him again.
While it was still daylight, the people urged David to eat. But he swore, “May God deal with me severely if I taste bread or anything else before the sun goes down.”
The people took notice and were pleased. Everything the king did pleased them.
That day everyone there and all Israel understood that the king hadn't ordered Abner son of Ner killed.
The king asked his servants, “Don't you know a ruler and a great man fell in Israel today?
Today I'm weak, even though I've been anointed king. These sons of Zeruiah are too hard for me to handle. May the LORD repay whoever did this evil for what he's done.”
When Saul's son Ishbosheth heard that Abner had died at Hebron, he lost his courage, and all Israel was shaken.
Two men commanded his raiding bands. Their names were Baanah and Rechab, sons of Rimmon from Beeroth in Benjamin. Beeroth is counted as part of Benjamin,
though its people fled to Gittaim, where they've lived as foreigners ever since.

Saul's son Jonathan had a son who couldn't walk normally. He was five years old when news about Saul and Jonathan came from Jezreel. His nurse picked him up and ran, but in her hurry he fell and injured his feet. His name was Mephibosheth.
Rechab and Baanah, sons of Rimmon from Beeroth, went to Ishbosheth's house during the hottest part of the day, while he was resting at noon.
They went into the middle of the house as if to collect wheat. They struck Ishbosheth and escaped.
They had gone into his bedroom while he was lying on his bed, killed him, and cut off his head. Then they took his head and traveled through the Arabah all night.

They brought Ishbosheth's head to David at Hebron and said, “Here's the head of Ishbosheth son of Saul, the enemy who wanted you dead. Today the LORD has avenged my lord the king against Saul and his descendants.”
David answered Rechab and his brother Baanah, the sons of Rimmon from Beeroth, “As surely as the LORD lives, the one who has rescued me from every trouble,
when a man told me, ‘Saul is dead,’ he thought he was bringing good news. I seized him and put him to death in Ziklag. That was his reward for the news.
How much more should I hold you accountable? Wicked men have murdered an innocent man in his own house, on his own bed. I'll answer for his blood by removing you from the earth.”
David ordered his young men to execute them. They cut off their hands and feet and hung their bodies beside the pool at Hebron. They buried Ishbosheth's head in Abner's grave at Hebron.
All the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and said, “We're your own flesh and blood.
Even when Saul was king over us, you were the one leading Israel out and bringing it back. The LORD told you, ‘You'll shepherd my people Israel and become their ruler.’”
All Israel's elders came to King David at Hebron. He made a covenant with them there before the LORD, and they anointed him king over Israel.
David was thirty years old when he became king. He reigned for forty years.
He ruled Judah from Hebron for seven years and six months. From Jerusalem he ruled all Israel and Judah for thirty-three years.
The king and his men went to Jerusalem to fight the Jebusites who lived there. The Jebusites told him, “Even the blind and the lame will keep you out.” They thought David couldn't get into the city.
But David captured the stronghold of Zion, which became the City of David.

That day David said, “Whoever takes on the Jebusites must go up by the watercourse and strike those ‘lame and blind’ whom David hates.” That's where the saying comes from: “The blind and the lame can't enter the house.”
David moved into the stronghold and named it the City of David. He built up the area from the Millo inward.
David grew more and more powerful because the LORD, the God of Armies, was with him.
King Hiram of Tyre sent messengers to David with cedar, carpenters, and stoneworkers. They built David a house.
David realized that the LORD had established him as Israel's king and had raised up his kingdom for the sake of his people Israel.
After moving from Hebron, David took more wives and concubines in Jerusalem. He had more sons and daughters.
These are the names of the children born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon,
Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia,
Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet.
When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, they all went looking for him. David heard about it and went down to the stronghold.
The Philistines had spread out across the Valley of Rephaim.
David asked the LORD, “Should I go up against the Philistines? Will you hand them over to me?” The LORD said, “Go up. I'll certainly hand them over to you.”
David went to Baal Perazim and defeated them there. He said, “The LORD broke through my enemies like water bursting through a barrier.” That's why he named the place Baal Perazim.
The Philistines left their idols behind, and David and his men carried them away.
The Philistines came up again and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim.
David asked the LORD what to do. The LORD told him to go around behind the Philistines and come against them near the mulberry trees.
When he heard marching in the treetops, he was to move, because the LORD would have gone ahead of him to strike down the Philistine army.
David did what the LORD commanded and struck down the Philistines all the way from Geba to Gezer.
David gathered Israel's chosen men again, thirty thousand in all.
He and everyone with him set out from Baale Judah to bring back God's ark. It bears the name of the LORD of Armies, who sits enthroned above the cherubim.
They put God's ark on a new cart and brought it out of Abinadab's house on the hill. His sons Uzzah and Ahio drove the cart.
They brought God's ark out from the house on the hill, and Ahio walked ahead of it.
David and all Israel made music before the LORD with every kind of cypress-wood instrument, including harps, stringed instruments, tambourines, castanets, and cymbals.
When they reached Nacon's threshing floor, the oxen stumbled, so Uzzah reached out and grabbed God's ark.
The LORD was furious with Uzzah. God struck him there for what he had done, and he died beside the ark.
David was upset because the LORD had struck Uzzah. He named the place Perez Uzzah, and it still goes by that name.
David was afraid of the LORD that day. “How can I bring the LORD's ark to my city?” he asked.
So David decided against taking the ark into David's City. He took it to the home of Obed-Edom from Gath instead.
The LORD's ark stayed with Obed-Edom from Gath for three months, and the LORD blessed him and his whole household.
Word reached King David that the LORD had blessed Obed-Edom's household and everything he owned because of God's ark. So David went to get the ark and brought it into David's City with joy.
After the people carrying the LORD's ark had gone six steps, David sacrificed an ox and a fattened calf.
David wore a linen ephod and danced before the LORD with all his strength.
David and all Israel brought up the LORD's ark with loud cheers and the blast of a trumpet.
As the ark entered David's City, Saul's daughter Michal looked out the window. She saw King David jumping and dancing before the LORD and felt nothing but contempt for him.
They brought in the LORD's ark and set it in the middle of the tent David had put up for it. David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD.
After presenting the offerings, David blessed the people in the name of the LORD of Armies.
He gave every man and woman in the crowd of Israelites a portion of bread, dates, and raisins. Then everyone went home.

When David came home to bless his household, Saul's daughter Michal came out to meet him. “How dignified the king of Israel looked today, exposing himself in front of his servants' maids like a shameless fool!”
David answered Michal, “I was dancing before the LORD, who chose me over your father and his entire family to lead Israel, his people. I'll keep celebrating before the LORD.
I'll make an even bigger fool of myself and think nothing of my own status. But those maids you just mentioned will honor me.”
Saul's daughter Michal never had a child.
The king settled into his palace, and the LORD gave him peace from all the enemies around him.
He said to Nathan the prophet, “Here I am living in a cedar palace while God's ark stays behind curtains.”
Nathan told the king, “Go ahead with what's on your heart. The LORD is with you.”
But that night the LORD gave Nathan this message:
“Go tell my servant David, ‘This is what the LORD says: Are you the one to build me a house to live in?
I haven't lived in a house from the day I brought Israel out of Egypt until now. I've moved from place to place in a tent, a portable sanctuary.
Everywhere I went with Israel, did I ever ask any of the tribal leaders I appointed to shepherd my people, “Why haven't you built me a cedar house?”’
“Now tell my servant David, ‘This is what the LORD of Armies says: I took you out of the sheep pen, away from tending sheep, to lead my people Israel.
I've been with you wherever you've gone, and I've cut down every enemy in your way. I'll make your name as great as the names of the greatest people on earth.
I'll choose a place for my people Israel and plant them there. They'll live on their own land without being driven out again. Violent people will no longer oppress them as they did at first,
back when I appointed judges over my people Israel. I'll give you peace from all your enemies. The LORD also tells you that he will build you a house, a royal family.
When your time is up and you rest with your ancestors, I'll raise up one of your own descendants to succeed you, and I'll establish his kingdom.
He will build a house for my name, and I will establish his royal throne forever.
I will be his father, and he will be my son. If he does wrong, I'll discipline him through ordinary human punishment, with rods and blows.
But my faithful love won't leave him the way it left Saul, whom I removed before you.
Your house and kingdom will stand secure before you forever. Your throne will stand forever.’”
Nathan told David everything the LORD had said and everything he had seen in the vision.
King David went in and sat before the LORD. “Who am I, Lord GOD, and who is my family, that you've brought me this far?
And as if this were a small thing to you, Lord GOD, you've also spoken about the distant future of my family. You've made this known among people, Lord GOD!
What more can I say to you? You know me, your servant, Lord GOD.
To keep your word and carry out what you wanted, you've done these great things and made them known to me.
That's why you are great, LORD God. From everything we've heard with our own ears, there's no one like you and no God besides you.

What other nation on earth is like your people Israel? You went to rescue them as your own people and make a name for yourself. You did great and awe-inspiring things for your land before the people you rescued out of Egypt, from the nations and their gods.
You made Israel your own people forever, and you, LORD, became their God.
“Now, LORD God, keep forever the promise you made about me and my family. Do what you said you would do.
May your name be honored forever, so people say, ‘The LORD of Armies is God over Israel.’ May the house of your servant David stand firm before you.
You, LORD of Armies, God of Israel, told your servant, ‘I will build you a house.’ That's why I found the courage to pray this prayer to you.
“Lord GOD, you are God. Your words are true, and you've promised this good thing to me, your servant.
Please bless my family so it will stand before you forever. You have spoken, Lord GOD. With your blessing, my family will be blessed forever.”
After this David defeated the Philistines, brought them under his rule, and took control of their principal city.

David defeated Moab and made the captives lie on the ground. He measured them off with a line, putting two lengths to death and sparing one full length. The Moabites became his subjects and paid him tribute.
David also defeated Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah, as Hadadezer went to restore his rule at the Euphrates.
David captured seventeen hundred horsemen and twenty thousand foot soldiers. He hamstrung the chariot horses but kept enough for a hundred chariots.
When the Syrians from Damascus came to help King Hadadezer of Zobah, David struck down twenty-two thousand of them.
David stationed troops in the territory of Damascus. The Syrians became his subjects and paid him tribute. The LORD gave David victory wherever he went.
David took the gold shields carried by Hadadezer's servants and brought them to Jerusalem.
King David took a large amount of bronze from Betah and Berothai, two of Hadadezer's cities.
When King Toi of Hamath heard that David had defeated Hadadezer's whole army,
he sent his son Joram to greet King David and congratulate him on defeating Hadadezer, who had been at war with Toi. Joram brought objects made of silver, gold, and bronze.
King David dedicated these to the LORD along with the silver and gold he had set apart from all the nations he'd subdued.
They came from Syria, Moab, Ammon, the Philistines, and Amalek, and from the plunder of Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah.
David made a name for himself when he returned from striking down eighteen thousand Syrians in the Valley of Salt.
David stationed troops all across Edom, and all the Edomites became his subjects. The LORD gave David victory wherever he went.
David ruled over all Israel and did what was just and right for all his people.
Joab son of Zeruiah commanded the army, and Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud kept the official records.
Zadok son of Ahitub and Ahimelech son of Abiathar were priests, and Seraiah was the scribe.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada commanded the Cherethites and Pelethites, and David's sons served as chief ministers.
David asked, “Is anyone from Saul's family still alive? I'd like to show them kindness for Jonathan's sake.”
Saul's household had a servant named Ziba. He was called in to see David, and the king asked, “Are you Ziba?” He answered, “I'm your servant.”
The king asked, “Is anyone left from Saul's family that I can show God's kindness to?” Ziba answered, “Jonathan still has a son. He has a disability in both feet.”
“Where is he?” the king asked. Ziba said, “He's at the home of Machir son of Ammiel in Lo Debar.”
So King David sent for him and had him brought from the home of Machir son of Ammiel in Lo Debar.
When Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son and Saul's grandson, came to David, he bowed with his face to the ground to show respect. David said, “Mephibosheth?” He answered, “Here I am, your servant.”
David said, “Don't be afraid. I'll show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan. I'll give back all the land that belonged to your grandfather Saul, and you'll always eat at my table.”
Mephibosheth bowed and said, “Who am I, your servant, that you'd pay attention to a dead dog like me?”
The king called Saul's servant Ziba and told him, “I've given your master's grandson everything that belonged to Saul and his family.

You, your sons, and your servants will farm his land and bring in the harvest so your master's grandson has food. Mephibosheth himself will always eat at my table.” Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.
Ziba told the king, “I'll do everything my lord the king has commanded.” So Mephibosheth ate at the king's table like one of the king's sons.
Mephibosheth had a young son named Mica. Everyone in Ziba's household served Mephibosheth.
Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem and ate regularly at the king's table. He had a disability in both feet.
After this the king of Ammon died, and his son Hanun took his place.

David said, “I'll show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, just as his father showed kindness to me.” So he sent his servants to comfort Hanun after his father's death, and they entered Ammonite territory.
But the Ammonite leaders said to their king Hanun, “Do you really think David sent these men to honor your father? He's sent his servants to scout the city, spy on it, and overthrow it!”
Hanun seized David's servants, shaved off half of each man's beard, cut their clothes at the waist so their backsides were exposed, and sent them away.
When David heard what had happened, he sent people to meet the men because they were deeply ashamed. The king told them, “Stay in Jericho until your beards grow back, then return.”

When the Ammonites realized David was disgusted with them, they hired twenty thousand Syrian foot soldiers from Beth Rehob and Zobah, the king of Maacah with a thousand men, and twelve thousand men from Tob.
When David heard this, he sent Joab with the whole army of his best fighters.
The Ammonites came out and lined up for battle at the city gate. The Syrians from Zobah and Rehob and the men from Tob and Maacah stood apart in the open field.
Joab saw that he faced battle from the front and the rear, so he picked some of Israel's best fighters and lined them up against the Syrians.
He put the rest of his forces under his brother Abishai, who lined them up against the Ammonites.
Joab said, “If the Syrians are too strong for me, come help me. If the Ammonites are too strong for you, I'll come help you.
Take courage. Let's fight bravely for our people and for the cities of our God. May the LORD do what he sees fit.”
Joab and his men advanced to fight the Syrians, and the Syrians ran from them.
When the Ammonites saw the Syrians running, they fled from Abishai into the city. Joab broke off the fight against the Ammonites and went back to Jerusalem.
When the Syrians realized Israel had defeated them, they regrouped.
Hadadezer summoned the Syrians from across the Euphrates. They came to Helam under Shobach, the commander of Hadadezer's army.
When David heard this, he gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, and came to Helam. The Syrians lined up against David and fought him.
The Syrians fled from Israel. David killed seven hundred Syrian chariot fighters and forty thousand horsemen. He struck down their commander Shobach, who died there.
When all the kings who served Hadadezer saw that Israel had defeated them, they made peace with Israel and became its subjects. The Syrians were afraid to help the Ammonites again.

When the year came around to the season kings went to war, David sent Joab out with his officers and all Israel's army. They devastated Ammon and laid siege to Rabbah, while David stayed in Jerusalem.
One evening David got up from his bed and walked across the palace roof. From there he saw a woman bathing. She was very beautiful.
David sent someone to find out who she was. The report came back, “Isn't that Bathsheba, Eliam's daughter and the wife of Uriah the Hittite?”
David sent messengers to bring her to him. She came to him and he slept with her. She had purified herself from her ritual uncleanness. Then she went back home.
She became pregnant and sent David a message: “I'm pregnant.”
David sent word to Joab: “Send me Uriah the Hittite.” So Joab sent Uriah to David.
When Uriah came in, David asked how Joab was doing, how the troops were holding up, and how the war was going.
David told Uriah, “Go home and wash your feet.” Uriah left the palace, and the king sent a gift after him.
But Uriah slept at the palace entrance alongside his master's servants. He never went home.
When David heard that Uriah hadn't gone home, he asked him, “You've just come back from a journey. Why didn't you go to your house?”

Uriah answered, “The ark and the troops of Israel and Judah are staying in tents. My commander Joab and my master's servants are camped out in the open. How could I go home to eat, drink, and sleep with my wife? As surely as you live, I won't do that.”
David said, “Stay here one more day. I'll send you back tomorrow.” So Uriah stayed in Jerusalem that day and the next.
David invited him to eat and drink with him and got him drunk. That evening Uriah went out to sleep alongside his master's servants again. He still didn't go home.
The next morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it with Uriah.
In the letter he wrote, “Put Uriah at the front where the fighting is fiercest, then pull back from him so he gets struck down and dies.”
While Joab was watching the city, he assigned Uriah to the place where he knew the strongest defenders were.
The men of the city came out and fought Joab. Some of David's men fell, and Uriah the Hittite died too.
Joab sent David a full report on the fighting.
He gave the messenger these instructions: “When you've finished reporting the fighting to the king,
he may get angry and ask, ‘Why did you fight so close to the city? Didn't you know they'd shoot at you from the wall?

Who killed Abimelech son of Jerubbesheth? A woman dropped an upper millstone on him from the wall and he died at Thebez. Why did you get so close to the wall?’ Then tell him, ‘Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead too.’”
The messenger went to David and told him everything Joab had sent him to report.
He said, “The men had the upper hand and came out into the open to fight us, but we drove them back as far as the city gate.
Then archers shot at your men from the wall. Some of the king's men are dead, and your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead too.”
David told the messenger, “Say to Joab, ‘Don't let this get to you. The sword takes one person as easily as another. Press the attack and take the city.’ Give him some encouragement.”
When Uriah's wife heard that her husband had died, she mourned for him.
When her time of mourning ended, David brought her to his palace. She became his wife and bore him a son. But the LORD was displeased with what David had done.
The LORD sent Nathan to David. Nathan came in and said, “Two men lived in the same city. One was rich and the other was poor.
The rich man owned many flocks and herds.

The poor man had nothing except one little ewe lamb he had bought. He raised her, and she grew up with him and his children. She ate his food, drank from his cup, and curled up in his arms. She was like a daughter to him.
A traveler came to visit the rich man. The rich man wouldn't take an animal from his own flock or herd to cook for his guest. He took the poor man's lamb and prepared it for the traveler.”
David was furious. “As surely as the LORD lives,” he told Nathan, “the man who did this deserves to die!
He has to pay back four times what he took, because he did this without a shred of pity!”
Nathan told David, “You're that man! This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘I anointed you king over Israel and rescued you from Saul.
I gave you your master's household and his wives, and I gave you Israel and Judah. If that had been too little, I'd have given you even more.
Why did you treat the LORD's word with contempt and do what he sees as evil? You struck down Uriah the Hittite and took his wife as your own. You used the sword of the Ammonites to kill him.
So now the sword will never leave your family, because you treated me with contempt and took Uriah the Hittite's wife as your own.’

“This is what the LORD says: ‘I will bring trouble against you from within your own family. Right in front of you I will take your wives and give them to someone close to you, and he will sleep with them in broad daylight.
You did this in secret, but I will do this in broad daylight before all Israel.’”
David told Nathan, “I've sinned against the LORD.” Nathan replied, “The LORD has taken away your sin. You won't die.
But what you did gave the LORD's enemies plenty of reason to speak against him. The child born to you will surely die.”
Then Nathan went home. The LORD struck the child Uriah's wife had borne to David, and the child became very sick.
David pleaded with God for the child. He fasted, went inside, and lay on the ground all night.
The elders of his household stood beside him and tried to help him up, but he refused to get up or eat with them.

On the seventh day the child died. David's servants were afraid to tell him. “When the child was alive, he wouldn't listen to us,” they said. “What if he hurts himself when we tell him the child is dead?”
David saw his servants whispering and realized what had happened. “Is the child dead?” he asked. They said, “He is.”
David got up from the ground, washed, put oil on himself, and changed his clothes. He went to the LORD's house to worship. Then he went home, asked for food, and ate what they brought him.
His servants asked, “Why are you doing this? While the child was alive you fasted and cried. Now that he's dead, you've gotten up and eaten.”
David said, “While the child was alive, I fasted and cried because I thought, ‘Who knows? The LORD might show me mercy and let the child live.’
But now he's dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back? I'll go to him, but he won't come back to me.”
David comforted his wife Bathsheba and slept with her. She gave birth to a son, and David named him Solomon. The LORD loved him.
The LORD sent word through Nathan the prophet to name him Jedidiah, because the LORD loved him.
Meanwhile, Joab fought against Rabbah in Ammon and seized the royal city.
Joab sent messengers to David: “I've fought against Rabbah and captured the part of the city that controls its water.
Now gather the rest of the troops, surround the city, and take it yourself. Otherwise I'll take it and the city will be called by my name.”
So David gathered all the troops, went to Rabbah, fought against it, and captured it.
David took the crown off their king's head. It weighed a talent of gold and was set with precious stones. It was placed on David's head, and he took a great deal of plunder out of the city.

David brought the people out and put them to work with saws, iron picks, and iron axes, and made them work at the brick kiln. He did this in all the Ammonite cities. Then David and all the troops returned to Jerusalem.
After this, David's son Amnon fell in love with Tamar, the beautiful sister of David's son Absalom.
Amnon worked himself sick over his sister Tamar. She was a virgin, and he couldn't see how to get to her.
Amnon had a friend named Jonadab, the son of David's brother Shimeah. Jonadab was a shrewd man.
He asked Amnon, “Why do you look so miserable every day? You're the king's son. Won't you tell me?” Amnon answered, “I'm in love with Tamar, my brother Absalom's sister.”

Jonadab told him, “Get into bed and pretend you're sick. When your father visits, say, ‘Please send my sister Tamar to give me something to eat. Let her prepare it where I can see and feed me herself.’”
Amnon lay down and pretended to be sick. When the king visited, Amnon said, “Please let my sister Tamar come and make a couple of cakes where I can see her, so she can feed me herself.”
David sent word to Tamar at home: “Go to your brother Amnon's house and make him something to eat.”
So Tamar went to Amnon's house and found him lying down. She took some dough, kneaded it, shaped the cakes where he could see her, and baked them.
She tipped the cakes out of the pan in front of him, but he refused to eat. “Send everyone out,” Amnon said, and everyone left.
Then Amnon told Tamar, “Bring the food into the bedroom so you can feed me.” Tamar took the cakes she'd made and brought them into her brother's room.
When Tamar brought the food close, he grabbed her and said, “Come to bed with me, my sister.”
“No, my brother,” she pleaded. “Don't force me. People in Israel must never do such a thing. Don't do this disgraceful thing!
Where could I go with my shame? And you'd be known as one of Israel's worst fools. Please speak to the king. He won't refuse to let you marry me.”
Amnon refused to listen. He was stronger than Tamar, and he raped her.
Then Amnon hated her. His hatred for her was stronger than the love he'd felt before. “Get up and get out!” he told her.
Tamar answered, “No! Sending me away like this is even worse than what you already did to me.” He refused to listen.
He called the servant who attended him and said, “Throw this woman out and bolt the door behind her.”
Tamar was wearing a robe of many colors, the kind the king's unmarried daughters wore. Amnon's servant put her out and bolted the door behind her.
Tamar put ashes on her head and tore her colorful robe. She put her hand on her head and went away crying out loud.
Her brother Absalom asked, “Has your brother Amnon been with you? For now, my sister, keep quiet. He's your brother. Don't take this to heart.” Tamar stayed in her brother Absalom's house, desolate.
King David heard what happened and was furious.
Absalom said nothing to Amnon, good or bad. He hated Amnon for raping his sister Tamar.
Two full years later, Absalom had sheep shearers working at Baal Hazor near Ephraim. He invited all the king's sons.
Absalom went to the king and said, “My sheep shearers are here. Please come with your servants and join me.”
The king answered, “No, my son. If we all come, we'll be a burden to you.” Absalom pressed him, but David stayed behind and gave him his blessing.
Absalom said, “If you won't come, please let my brother Amnon come with us.” The king asked, “Why should he go with you?”
Absalom kept asking until David let Amnon and all the king's sons go with him.
Absalom ordered his servants, “Watch for Amnon to get merry with wine. When I say, ‘Strike Amnon,’ kill him. Don't be afraid. I'm the one giving the order. Be brave and do it.”
Absalom's servants killed Amnon as ordered. All the other sons of the king jumped up, mounted their mules, and fled.
While they were still on the road, word reached David: “Absalom has killed all the king's sons. None of them survived!”
The king stood up, tore his clothes, and lay on the ground. All his servants stood around him with their clothes torn.
But Jonadab, son of David's brother Shimeah, said, “My lord, don't assume they've killed all the king's sons. Amnon alone is dead. Absalom had planned this since the day Amnon raped his sister Tamar.
So don't take it to heart, my lord the king. Your sons haven't all died. Only Amnon is dead.”
Meanwhile Absalom fled. The young man on watch looked up and saw a crowd coming down the road along the hillside behind him.
Jonadab said to the king, “Look, your sons are coming. It's just as your servant told you.”
As soon as he finished speaking, the king's sons arrived, weeping loudly. The king and all his servants wept bitterly too.
Absalom fled to Talmai son of Ammihur, the king of Geshur. David mourned for his son every day.
After escaping to Geshur, Absalom stayed there three years.
King David longed to go to Absalom, now that he had found some comfort after Amnon's death.
Joab son of Zeruiah realized that the king's heart was with Absalom.
Joab sent for a wise woman from Tekoa. He told her, “Pretend you're grieving. Put on mourning clothes and don't put oil on yourself. Look like a woman who's been mourning someone for a long time.
Go to the king and say what I tell you.” Then Joab gave her the words to say.
When the woman from Tekoa went to speak to the king, she bowed with her face to the ground. “Help me, Your Majesty!” she said.
“What's troubling you?” the king asked. She answered, “I'm a widow. My husband is dead.
I had two sons, and they got into a fight out in the field. Nobody was there to pull them apart, and one struck and killed the other.

Now my whole family has turned against me. They say, ‘Hand over the one who struck his brother, so we can kill him for taking his brother's life.’ That would wipe out the heir too. They'd put out the one ember I have left, leaving my husband without a name or anyone to carry it on anywhere on earth.”
The king told the woman, “Go home, and I'll give orders about your case.”
The woman from Tekoa said, “My lord the king, may the guilt fall on me and my father's family. May the king and his throne be free of blame.”
The king said, “If anyone says a word against you, bring him to me, and he won't trouble you again.”

“Please remember the LORD your God,” she said. “Stop the one seeking revenge from taking another life, or they'll kill my son.” David said, “As surely as the LORD lives, not one hair of your son's head will fall to the ground.”
The woman said, “Please let me say one more thing to my lord the king.” He said, “Go ahead.”
She asked, “Then why have you planned something like this against God's people? By what you've just said, you've shown yourself at fault, because you haven't brought back the one you sent away.
We all have to die. We're like water spilled on the ground that can never be gathered up again. Yet God doesn't take away life. He finds a way for someone who has been banished to come back to him.
I came to say this to you, my lord the king, because the people frightened me. I thought, ‘I'll speak to the king. Maybe he'll do what I ask.
Surely he'll listen and rescue me from the man who wants to cut off both me and my son from the inheritance God gave us.’
Then I thought, ‘May my lord the king's word give me peace. My lord the king is like an angel of God in knowing right from wrong. May the LORD your God be with you.’”
The king answered the woman, “Please don't hold anything back when I ask you this.” She replied, “Go ahead, my lord the king.”

“Is Joab behind all this?” the king asked. The woman answered, “As surely as you live, my lord the king, nobody could get around what you've just said. Your servant Joab sent me and told me everything to say.
Joab did this to change how you saw the situation. My lord has wisdom like an angel of God and knows everything that goes on in the land.”
The king told Joab, “All right, I've granted your request. Go and bring the young man Absalom back.”
Joab bowed with his face to the ground, showed the king respect, and blessed him. He said, “Today I know I've found favor with you, my lord the king, because you've granted my request.”
So Joab went to Geshur and brought Absalom back to Jerusalem.
But the king said, “Let him go to his own house. He must stay away from me.” Absalom went home and didn't see the king.
Everyone in Israel praised Absalom for his looks more than anyone else. From head to toe, there wasn't a flaw in him.
He cut his hair at the end of each year because it got too heavy. When he weighed what he'd cut off, it came to two hundred shekels by the royal standard.
Absalom had three sons and one daughter named Tamar. She was beautiful.
Absalom lived in Jerusalem for two full years without seeing the king.
He sent for Joab so he could send him to the king, but Joab wouldn't come. Absalom sent for him a second time, and he still wouldn't come.
So Absalom told his servants, “Joab's barley field is right next to mine. Go set it on fire.” They set the field on fire.
Joab went to Absalom's house and asked him, “Why did your servants set my field on fire?”

Absalom answered, “I sent word asking you to come so I could have you ask the king, ‘Why did I come back from Geshur? I'd be better off still there. Let me see the king now, and if I'm guilty, let him put me to death.’”
Joab went to the king and told him. The king sent for Absalom, who came in and bowed with his face to the ground before him. Then the king kissed Absalom.
After this, Absalom got himself a chariot and horses, with fifty men to run ahead of him.

He got up early and stood by the road to the city gate. Whenever someone came to have the king rule on a dispute, Absalom called out, “What town are you from?” The person would say which tribe of Israel he belonged to.
Absalom would tell him, “You've got a valid case, but the king hasn't appointed anyone to hear you.”
Then he'd say, “If only I were made judge in this land! Anyone with a dispute could come to me, and I'd see that they got justice.”
Whenever someone came up to bow to him, Absalom would reach out, take hold of him, and kiss him.
Absalom treated all the Israelites who came to the king for a ruling this way. That's how he stole the hearts of the people of Israel.
At the end of forty years, Absalom said to the king, “Please let me go to Hebron to fulfill a vow I made to the LORD.
While I was staying in Geshur in Syria, I vowed, ‘If the LORD really brings me back to Jerusalem, I'll serve him.’”
“Go in peace,” the king told him. So Absalom left for Hebron.
But Absalom sent spies through all the tribes of Israel with this message: “As soon as you hear the trumpet, say, ‘Absalom is king in Hebron!’”
Two hundred men from Jerusalem went with Absalom as invited guests. They went in good faith and knew nothing about the plot.
While Absalom was offering sacrifices, he sent to Giloh for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's adviser. The conspiracy gained strength as more and more people joined Absalom.
A messenger came to David and said, “The people of Israel have given their hearts to Absalom.”

David told all his servants with him in Jerusalem, “Get up! We have to run, or none of us will escape from Absalom. Hurry, before he catches us, brings disaster on us, and attacks the city with the sword.”
The king's servants answered, “We're ready to do whatever my lord the king decides.”
The king left with his whole household following him. He left ten of his concubines behind to look after the palace.
The king went out with all the people following, and they stopped at Beth Merhak.
All his servants filed past him, including all the Cherethites and Pelethites. The six hundred Gittites who had followed him from Gath also marched past the king.
The king asked Ittai from Gath, “Why are you coming with us too? Go back and stay with the king. You're a foreigner and an exile. Go back to where you've been living.
You only came yesterday. Should I make you wander with us today when I don't even know where I'm going? Go back and take your people with you. May mercy and faithfulness be with you.”
Ittai answered the king, “As surely as the LORD lives and as surely as my lord the king lives, wherever you are, your servant will be there too, whether it means life or death.”
David told Ittai, “Go ahead and cross.” So Ittai from Gath crossed over with all his men and the children who were with him.
Everyone in the countryside wept aloud as the people passed. The king himself crossed the Kidron Valley stream, and all the people went across toward the wilderness.
Zadok came too, with all the Levites carrying the ark of God's covenant. They set God's ark down, and Abiathar went up while the last of the people made their way out of the city.
The king told Zadok, “Take God's ark back to the city. If the LORD looks on me with favor, he'll bring me back and let me see it again and the place where he dwells.
But if he says, ‘I take no delight in you,’ here I am. Let him do whatever he sees fit with me.”
The king also told Zadok the priest, “Aren't you a seer? Go back into the city in peace with the two young men, your son Ahimaaz and Abiathar's son Jonathan.
I'll wait at the wilderness crossings until you send me word.”
So Zadok and Abiathar took God's ark back to Jerusalem and stayed there.
David climbed the Mount of Olives weeping, with his head covered and his feet bare. Everyone with him covered their heads and wept as they went up.
Someone told David, “Ahithophel is part of Absalom's plot.” David prayed, “LORD, please turn Ahithophel's advice into foolishness.”
When David reached the summit, where people worshiped God, Hushai the Archite came to meet him with his tunic torn and dirt on his head.
David told him, “If you come with me, you'll be a burden.
But if you go back to the city and tell Absalom, ‘I'll serve you, Your Majesty. Just as I served your father before, I'll serve you now,’ you can undermine Ahithophel's advice for me.
You'll have the priests Zadok and Abiathar there. Tell them everything you hear from the palace.
Their two sons are there with them, Ahimaaz son of Zadok and Jonathan son of Abiathar. Send me everything you hear through them.”
So Hushai, David's friend, entered the city as Absalom arrived in Jerusalem.

Just past the summit, David met Ziba, Mephibosheth's servant. He had two saddled donkeys loaded with two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred clusters of raisins, a hundred summer fruits, and a container of wine.

The king asked Ziba, “What's all this for?” Ziba said, “The donkeys are for your household to ride. The bread and fruit are for the young men to eat, and the wine is for anyone who grows faint in the wilderness.”
“Where is your master's grandson?” the king asked. Ziba answered, “He's staying in Jerusalem. He said, ‘Today the people of Israel will give me back my family's kingdom.’”
The king told Ziba, “Everything that belongs to Mephibosheth is yours now.” Ziba said, “I bow before you. May I find favor with you, my lord the king.”
When King David reached Bahurim, a man from Saul's family came out. His name was Shimei son of Gera, and he came out cursing.
He threw stones at David and all his servants, even though the people and the king's best fighters were on either side of him.
Shimei shouted curses at him: “Get out! Get out, you bloodthirsty man, you villain!

The LORD is making you pay for all the blood shed in Saul's family, whose throne you took. The LORD has given the kingdom to your son Absalom. Your own evil has caught up with you because you've shed so much blood!”
Abishai son of Zeruiah asked the king, “Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over there and cut off his head.”
The king answered, “What business is this of yours, you sons of Zeruiah? If he's cursing because the LORD told him, ‘Curse David,’ who can ask him why he's doing it?”
David told Abishai and all his servants, “My own son wants me dead. Why be surprised that this man from Benjamin does too? Leave him alone and let him curse. The LORD has told him to.
Maybe the LORD will see the wrong done to me and repay me with good for the curses I've heard today.”
David and his men kept going down the road. Shimei went along the opposite hillside, cursing David, throwing stones at him, and flinging dust.
The king and all the people with him arrived exhausted, and David rested there.
Meanwhile, Absalom and his followers from Israel entered Jerusalem, and Ahithophel was with him.
When David's friend Hushai the Archite came to Absalom, he said, “Long live the king! Long live the king!”
Absalom asked Hushai, “Is this how you show loyalty to your friend? Why didn't you go with him?”
Hushai answered, “I will belong to the one the LORD and these people and all Israel have chosen. I'll stay with him.
Besides, who should I serve? Shouldn't I serve his son? Just as I served your father, I'll serve you.”
Then Absalom turned to Ahithophel and said, “Tell us what you think we should do.”

Ahithophel replied, “Sleep with your father's concubines, the women he left to look after the palace. Then all Israel will hear that your father despises you, and everyone on your side will take courage.”
They put up a tent for Absalom on the palace roof, and he slept with his father's concubines in full view of Israel.
In those days people took Ahithophel's advice as seriously as if they'd asked God himself at the inner sanctuary. That's how both David and Absalom regarded everything Ahithophel advised.
Ahithophel also told Absalom, “Let me pick twelve thousand men and go after David tonight.
I'll catch him worn out and exhausted and frighten him. Everyone with him will run away. I'll strike down the king alone
and bring everyone else back to you. Once you've dealt with the one man you're after, it's as good as having everyone back. All the people will be at peace.”
Absalom and all Israel's elders liked the plan.
Then Absalom said, “Call Hushai the Archite too. Let's hear what he has to say.”
When Hushai came in, Absalom told him what Ahithophel had said and asked, “Should we do what he says? If you disagree, speak up.”
Hushai answered, “This time Ahithophel's advice is no good.”

He went on, “You know your father and his men. They're tough fighters and as fierce as a bear in the wild that's lost her cubs. Your father knows war. He won't spend the night with the rest of the people.
He's already hiding in a pit or somewhere else. If some of your men fall in the first attack, anyone who hears of it will say, ‘Absalom's followers are being slaughtered!’
Even the bravest man, with a heart like a lion's, will lose his nerve. All Israel knows your father is a mighty warrior and the men with him are brave fighters.
Here's my advice. Gather all Israel to you, from Dan to Beersheba, as many as the grains of sand by the sea, and lead them into battle yourself.
We'll catch up with him wherever he is and fall on him the way dew settles on the ground. Neither he nor any of his men will survive.
If he retreats into a city, all Israel will bring ropes and drag the city into the river until there's not even a pebble left.”
Absalom and all the Israelite men said, “Hushai the Archite's advice is better than Ahithophel's.” The LORD had decided to overturn Ahithophel's sound advice and bring disaster on Absalom.
Then Hushai told Zadok and Abiathar the priests, “Here's what Ahithophel told Absalom and the elders of Israel, and here's what I advised.
Send word to David right away: ‘Don't spend the night at the wilderness crossings. Get across, or the king and everyone with him could be wiped out.’”
Jonathan and Ahimaaz were staying near En Rogel. A servant woman would pass messages to them, and they would take the messages to King David. They couldn't risk being seen entering the city.
A boy spotted them and told Absalom. Both men hurried away to a house in Bahurim. The owner had a well in his courtyard, and the two went down into it.
The woman of the house covered the mouth of the well and spread crushed grain on top. Nobody noticed a thing.

Absalom's servants came to the house and asked her, “Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?” She told them, “They've crossed the stream.” The men searched, found no trace of them, and went back to Jerusalem.

After the men left, Ahimaaz and Jonathan climbed out of the well and went to King David. “Get up and cross the water quickly,” they told him. Then they explained what Ahithophel had advised against him.
David got up, and he and everyone with him crossed the Jordan. By daybreak, every last one of them had made it across.
When Ahithophel saw that his advice hadn't been followed, he saddled his donkey and went home to his town. He put his affairs in order and hanged himself. He died and was buried in his father's tomb.
David reached Mahanaim. Absalom crossed the Jordan with all his Israelite troops.
Absalom put Amasa in command of the army in Joab's place. Amasa was the son of Ithra the Israelite and Abigail daughter of Nahash. Abigail was the sister of Zeruiah, Joab's mother.
Absalom and Israel camped in the land of Gilead.
When David arrived in Mahanaim, Shobi son of Nahash from the Ammonite city of Rabbah, Machir son of Ammiel from Lo Debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim
brought beds, basins, clay pots, wheat, barley, flour, parched grain, beans, lentils, roasted grain,
honey, butter, sheep, and cheese from the herd for David and his people to eat. “These people have grown hungry, tired, and thirsty in the wilderness,” they said.
David counted the troops with him and appointed commanders over units of a thousand and units of a hundred.

He sent the troops out in three groups. A third went under Joab, a third under Joab's brother Abishai son of Zeruiah, and a third under Ittai from Gath. The king told the troops, “I'm going out with you myself.”

But they answered, “You can't come with us. If we run, they won't care about us. If half of us die, they still won't care. But you're worth ten thousand of us. It's better if you stay ready to help us from the city.”
The king told them, “I'll do whatever seems best to you.” He stood beside the gate as the troops marched out by hundreds and thousands.
The king ordered Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, “For my sake, be gentle with the young man Absalom.” All the troops heard what the king told the commanders about Absalom.
David's troops marched out to meet Israel, and the battle took place in the forest of Ephraim.
David's men defeated Israel there. Twenty thousand men were killed that day.
The battle spread across the whole countryside, and the forest claimed more lives that day than the sword did.

Absalom ran into David's men while riding his mule. The mule went under the thick branches of a big oak, and Absalom's head got caught in the tree. He hung between earth and sky while the mule kept going.
One man saw him and told Joab, “I saw Absalom hanging in an oak tree.”
Joab said, “You saw him? Why didn't you strike him down right there? I'd have given you ten pieces of silver and a sash.”

The man answered, “Even if you put a thousand pieces of silver in my hand, I wouldn't lay a hand on the king's son. We all heard the king tell you, Abishai, and Ittai, ‘See that nobody touches the young man Absalom.’
If I had gone against the order and killed him, the king would've found out. Nothing stays hidden from him, and you yourself would've turned against me.”
Joab said, “I'm done wasting time here with you.” He took three darts and drove them through Absalom's heart while he was still alive in the oak.
Ten young men who carried Joab's armor gathered around Absalom, struck him, and killed him.
Joab blew the trumpet and called his troops back. They stopped chasing Israel because Joab held them back.
They threw Absalom into a deep pit in the forest and piled a huge heap of stones over him. Everyone in Israel fled to their own tents.

While he was alive, Absalom had set up a pillar for himself in the King's Valley. He said, “I have no son to keep my name alive.” He named the pillar after himself, and it's still called Absalom's Monument.
Ahimaaz son of Zadok said, “Let me run and tell the king how the LORD brought him justice against his enemies.”
Joab replied, “You can carry news another day, but you won't carry it today. The king's son is dead.”
Then Joab told the Cushite, “Go tell the king what you saw.” The Cushite bowed to Joab and ran.
Ahimaaz son of Zadok asked Joab again, “Whatever happens, please let me run after the Cushite.” Joab said, “Why do you want to run, my son? You won't get a reward for this news.”
“Whatever happens, I'm going to run,” he said. “Run, then,” Joab replied. Ahimaaz took the route through the plain and outran the Cushite.
David was sitting between the two gates. The lookout climbed onto the gate roof by the wall, looked up, and saw a man running alone.
The lookout called down to the king. The king said, “If he's alone, he's carrying news.” The runner came closer and closer.
The lookout saw another man running and called to the gatekeeper, “Look, another man running alone!” The king said, “He's bringing news too.”
The lookout said, “The first one runs like Ahimaaz son of Zadok.” The king answered, “He's a good man. He's bringing good news.”

When Ahimaaz came near, he called out to the king, “All is well!” He bowed with his face to the ground and said, “Praise the LORD your God! He's handed over the men who rose up against my lord the king.”
The king asked, “Is the young man Absalom all right?” Ahimaaz answered, “When Joab sent me, the king's servant, I saw a great commotion, but I don't know what it was.”
The king said, “Step aside and stand here.” So he stepped aside and waited.
Then the Cushite arrived and said, “Good news for my lord the king! Today the LORD brought you justice against everyone who rose up against you.”
The king asked the Cushite, “Is the young man Absalom all right?” The Cushite answered, “May my lord the king's enemies and everyone who rises up to harm you end up like that young man.”
The king was shaken. He went up to the room over the gate and wept. As he went, he cried, “My son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I'd died instead of you! Absalom, my son, my son!”
Word reached Joab that the king was weeping and mourning for Absalom.
The day's victory turned into mourning for everyone when they heard that the king was grieving for his son.
The troops slipped into the city that day, like soldiers ashamed to be seen after running from a battle.
The king covered his face and cried aloud, “My son Absalom! Absalom, my son, my son!”
Joab went into the house and told the king, “Today you've humiliated everyone who saved your life and the lives of your sons and daughters, your wives, and your concubines.

You love those who hate you and hate those who love you. You've shown us today that your commanders and servants mean nothing to you. I can see you'd be happy if Absalom were alive and the rest of us had all died today.

Now get up, go outside, and say something to encourage your servants. I swear by the LORD that if you don't go out, nobody will stay with you tonight. That would be worse than anything that's happened to you since you were young.”
So the king got up and sat at the gate. Word went around that he was there, and everyone came before him. Meanwhile the Israelites who'd fought against him had fled to their tents.
People across all the tribes of Israel argued among themselves. “The king rescued us from our enemies and saved us from the Philistines,” they said. “Now he's fled the country because of Absalom.
And Absalom, whom we anointed to rule us, is dead in battle. Why is nobody talking about bringing the king back?”
King David sent word to the priests Zadok and Abiathar: “Ask the elders of Judah, ‘Why are you the last to bring the king home? All Israel is talking about bringing him back, and he's heard about it.
You're my brothers, my own flesh and bone. Why should you be the last to bring the king back?’
Tell Amasa, ‘Aren't you my own flesh and bone? May God punish me severely if I don't make you my permanent army commander in place of Joab.’”
David won over the people of Judah as one. They sent the king word: “Come back, you and all your servants.”
So the king started back and reached the Jordan. The people of Judah came to Gilgal to meet him and help him cross the river.
Shimei son of Gera, a man of Benjamin from Bahurim, hurried down with the people of Judah to meet King David.
A thousand men from Benjamin came with him. Ziba, the servant of Saul's household, came with his fifteen sons and twenty servants. They crossed the Jordan in front of the king.
A ferry went across to bring the king's household over and do whatever the king wanted. When the king had crossed the Jordan, Shimei son of Gera fell down before him.
He said, “My lord, please don't hold my guilt against me. Don't remember the wrong I did the day you left Jerusalem, and don't take it to heart.
I know I've sinned. That's why I've come down today to meet you, my lord the king, ahead of everyone else from the house of Joseph.”
Abishai son of Zeruiah answered, “Shouldn't Shimei die for cursing the LORD's anointed?”
David said, “What business is this of yours, you sons of Zeruiah? Why are you opposing me today? Should anyone be put to death in Israel today? I know I'm king over Israel again.”
The king told Shimei, “You won't die.” He gave him his oath.
Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson, also came down to meet the king. He hadn't cared for his feet, trimmed his beard, or washed his clothes from the day the king left until the day he returned safely.
When Mephibosheth came to Jerusalem to meet him, the king asked, “Why didn't you go with me?”
He answered, “My lord the king, my servant tricked me. I meant to saddle a donkey so I could ride and go with you, because I have a disability.
He lied about me to you, my lord the king. But you're like an angel of God, so do what seems right to you.
My whole family could have been put to death before you, my lord the king, yet you gave me a place among those who ate at your table. What right do I have to ask you for anything more?”
The king said to him, “Why say any more about it? I've decided that you and Ziba will divide the land.”
Mephibosheth told the king, “Let him take it all. My lord the king has come home safely.”
Barzillai the Gileadite came down from Rogelim and went across the Jordan with the king to see him safely over.
Barzillai was eighty years old. He was a wealthy man and had supplied what the king needed during his stay in Mahanaim.
The king said to Barzillai, “Cross over with me. I'll take care of you in Jerusalem.”
Barzillai answered, “How many years do I have left to live, that I should go up to Jerusalem with the king?
I'm eighty years old. Can I still tell good from bad? Can I taste what I eat or drink? Can I still hear men and women singing? Why should I be a burden to my lord the king?
I'll go just across the Jordan with you. Why should you give me such a reward?
Please let me go back and die in my own town near my parents' grave. But here's your servant Chimham. Let him cross with my lord the king, and treat him as you see fit.”
The king said, “Chimham will cross with me, and I'll do for him whatever you think best. I'll do anything you ask of me.”
All the people crossed the Jordan, and the king crossed too. Then he kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and Barzillai went back home.
The king went on to Gilgal with Chimham. All the people of Judah and half the people of Israel escorted him across.
Then the Israelites came to the king and asked, “Why did our brothers from Judah steal you away and take you, your household, and all your men across the Jordan?”
The men of Judah answered, “Because the king is our close relative. Why are you angry? Have we eaten at his expense? Has he given us any gift?”

The men of Israel answered, “We have ten shares in the king and a stronger claim to David than you have. Why did you treat us with contempt? Weren't we the first to suggest bringing our king back?” But the men of Judah answered even more harshly.

A troublemaker named Sheba son of Bichri, from the tribe of Benjamin, was there. He blew the trumpet and shouted, “We have no share in David and no inheritance in Jesse's son. Back to your tents, Israel!”
All the men of Israel stopped following David and followed Sheba son of Bichri. The men of Judah stayed with their king all the way from the Jordan to Jerusalem.

When David came home to Jerusalem, he took the ten concubines he'd left to look after the palace and put them under guard. He provided for them and never slept with them again. They lived in confinement as widows until they died.
The king told Amasa, “Call the men of Judah together for me within three days, and be back here yourself.”
So Amasa went to call up the men of Judah, but he took longer than the king had allowed.
David told Abishai, “Sheba son of Bichri is going to do us more harm than Absalom did. Take my men and go after him before he reaches fortified towns and gets away from us.”
Joab's men went with him, along with the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and the best fighters. They left Jerusalem to pursue Sheba son of Bichri.
At the great stone in Gibeon, Amasa came to meet them. Joab was in his battle clothes, with a sword strapped at his waist in its sheath. As he stepped forward, the sword slipped out.
Joab said, “How are you, my brother?” With his right hand he took Amasa by the beard to greet him with a kiss.

Amasa paid no attention to the sword in Joab's hand. Joab struck him in the belly, spilling his intestines onto the ground. Amasa died from that one blow. Joab and his brother Abishai went after Sheba son of Bichri.
One of Joab's young men stood by Amasa and called, “Whoever supports Joab and stands with David, follow Joab!”
Amasa lay in his blood in the middle of the road. The man saw that everyone who came by stopped, so he dragged Amasa off the road into a field and threw a garment over him.
Once Amasa was off the road, everyone followed Joab in pursuit of Sheba son of Bichri.
Sheba went through all the tribes of Israel to Abel in Beth Maacah. All the Berites came together and followed him there.
Joab's forces reached Abel of Beth Maacah and laid siege to Sheba there. They heaped up a siege ramp against the city's defenses and battering parties began trying to bring down the wall.
A wise woman called out from the city, “Listen! Listen! Tell Joab to come close. I need to speak to him.”
Joab came closer. “Are you Joab?” she asked. “I am,” he answered. She said, “Please listen to what I have to say.” He replied, “I'm listening.”
She told him, “In the old days people used to say, ‘Ask for advice at Abel,’ and that would settle the matter.
I'm one of Israel's peaceful and faithful people. You're trying to destroy a city that's like a mother in Israel. Why swallow up what belongs to the LORD?”
Joab answered, “I'd never dream of swallowing it up or destroying it.

Here's what's going on. A man from the hill country of Ephraim named Sheba son of Bichri has risen up against King David. Hand over that one man and I'll leave the city.” The woman answered, “His head will be thrown to you over the wall.”

The woman went to all the people with her wise advice. They cut off Sheba son of Bichri's head and threw it to Joab. He blew the trumpet, and his men withdrew from the city and went to their own tents. Joab went back to the king in Jerusalem.
Joab commanded Israel's whole army, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada commanded the Cherethites and Pelethites.
Adoram was in charge of forced labor, and Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud kept the official records.
Sheva was the scribe, and Zadok and Abiathar were priests.
Ira the Jairite was David's chief minister.

During David's reign there was a famine for three years in a row. David went to the LORD for an answer. The LORD said, “This is because of Saul and his bloodstained family. He put the Gibeonites to death.”

The king called the Gibeonites in to speak to them. They weren't Israelites but survivors of the Amorites. Israel had sworn to spare them, but Saul in his zeal for Israel and Judah had tried to kill them.
David asked the Gibeonites, “What can I do for you? How can I make things right so that you'll bless the people who belong to the LORD?”
They told him, “This isn't about money owed to us by Saul or his family. And we have no right to put anyone in Israel to death.” David said, “Tell me what you want me to do, and I'll do it.”
They answered the king, “There was a man who cut us down and plotted to wipe us out, so we'd have no place anywhere in Israel.
Hand over seven of his male descendants to us. We'll hang them before the LORD at Gibeah, the town of Saul, whom the LORD chose.” The king said, “I'll hand them over.”
But the king spared Mephibosheth son of Jonathan and grandson of Saul because of the oath David and Saul's son Jonathan had made to each other before the LORD.

Instead the king took Armoni and Mephibosheth, the two sons Rizpah daughter of Aiah had borne to Saul. He also took the five sons Saul's daughter Merab had borne to Adriel son of Barzillai from Meholah.

He handed them over to the Gibeonites, who hanged them on the mountain before the LORD. All seven died together. They were put to death in the first days of harvest, when the barley harvest was just beginning.

Rizpah daughter of Aiah spread sackcloth out on the rock for herself. From the start of harvest until rain poured down on the bodies, she kept the birds away by day and the wild animals away by night.
David heard what Rizpah daughter of Aiah, Saul's concubine, had done.

David went to get the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan from the people of Jabesh Gilead. They had stolen the bodies from the street in Beth Shan, where the Philistines had hung them after killing Saul at Gilboa.
David brought back the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan, and they gathered up the bones of the seven who had been hanged.
They buried Saul and Jonathan's bones in Zela, in the land of Benjamin, in the tomb of Saul's father Kish. They did everything the king commanded. After that, God answered prayer for the land.
The Philistines went to war with Israel again. David and his men went down and fought them, and David grew exhausted.
Ishbibenob was a descendant of the giant. His bronze spearhead weighed three hundred shekels, and he was armed with a new sword. He intended to kill David.
But Abishai son of Zeruiah came to David's aid and killed the Philistine. Then David's men swore to him, “You can't go into battle with us again. We can't let the lamp of Israel go out.”
Later there was another battle with the Philistines at Gob. Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Saph, another descendant of the giant.
In another battle with the Philistines at Gob, Elhanan son of Jaare-Oregim from Bethlehem killed the brother of Goliath from Gath. The shaft of his spear was as thick as a weaver's beam.
There was another battle at Gath. A huge man there had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four altogether. He too was a descendant of the giant.
He defied Israel, and Jonathan, the son of David's brother Shimei, killed him.
These four were descendants of the giant in Gath. They fell at the hands of David and his men.
David sang this song to the LORD when the LORD rescued him from Saul and from all his other enemies.
He said, “The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and the one who rescues me.
My God is the rock I run to for shelter. He's my shield, the mighty strength that saves me, my strong tower, and my refuge. You're my savior. You save me from violence.
I call out to the LORD, who deserves praise, and he saves me from my enemies.
Waves of death closed in around me. Floods of wickedness terrified me.
The ropes of the grave wrapped around me, and death's traps caught me.
In my trouble I called out to the LORD. I cried to my God. From his temple he heard my voice. My cry reached his ears.
Then the earth shook and trembled. The very foundations of heaven quaked and shook because he was angry.
Smoke rose from his nostrils. Fire poured from his mouth and set coals ablaze.
He bent the skies and came down with thick darkness under his feet.
He rode on a cherub and flew, appearing on the wings of the wind.
He wrapped himself in darkness like a shelter, with waters gathered in the thick clouds of the sky.
In the brightness ahead of him, coals burst into flame.
The LORD thundered from heaven. The Most High raised his voice.
He shot his arrows and scattered his enemies. His lightning threw them into confusion.
The channels of the sea came into view, and the world's foundations lay bare at the LORD's rebuke, at the blast of breath from his nostrils.
He reached down from high above and took hold of me. He pulled me out of deep waters.
He rescued me from my powerful enemy and from those who hated me, because they were too strong for me.
They came after me on the day disaster struck, but the LORD held me up.
He brought me out into a wide, open place. He rescued me because he delighted in me.
The LORD rewarded me for doing what was right. He repaid me because my hands were clean.
I've stayed on the LORD's paths and haven't turned away from my God to do wrong.
I've kept all his rulings in front of me and haven't strayed from what he commanded.
I've lived with integrity before him and kept myself from wrongdoing.
So the LORD rewarded me for doing what was right and for being clean in his sight.
To the merciful you show mercy, and to people of integrity you show your integrity.
To the pure you show yourself pure, and to the crooked you show yourself shrewd.
You save people who are suffering, and you keep your eyes on the arrogant to bring them down.
You are my lamp, LORD. The LORD lights up my darkness.
With your help I can charge a troop. With my God I can leap over a wall.
God's way is flawless. The LORD's word has stood the test. He's a shield to everyone who takes refuge in him.
Who is God besides the LORD? Who is a rock besides our God?
God is my strong fortress. He makes my path secure.
He gives me feet like a deer's and sets me high above the ground.
He trains my hands for battle so my arms can bend a bow of bronze.
You've given me your shield to save me. Your gentleness has made me great.
You've widened the path under my feet, and my footing hasn't slipped.
I chased my enemies and destroyed them. I didn't turn back until they were wiped out.
I struck them down until they couldn't get up. They fell beneath my feet.
You gave me strength for battle. You brought those who rose against me down beneath me.
You made my enemies turn and run, and I cut down those who hated me.
They looked for help, but nobody came to save them. They looked to the LORD, but he gave them no answer.
I ground them as fine as dust. I crushed them like mud in the streets and scattered them.
You rescued me from the conflicts of my own people. You kept me as ruler over nations. People I didn't know will serve me.
People from foreign lands will submit to me. As soon as they hear of me, they'll obey.
Their courage will fade, and they'll come out of hiding trembling.
The LORD lives! Praise my rock! Lift up God, the rock who saves me.
